name: Seashell hair removal

lead: Seashell hair removal refers to the prehistoric practice of using shells, flint and similar natural edges as primitive razors or tweezers to remove hair from the face and body.

The appearance payoff was a hairless, groomed look. Historical accounts describe hair removal for cleanliness as far back as prehistory, with flint and seashells among the earliest tools, long before metal razors or modern tweezers.

paras: Descriptions of the practice are general: a thin shell edge or knapped flint was scraped across the skin to cut hair, and paired shells were reportedly squeezed to pluck individual hairs. Today it is mainly a historical curiosity, with modern razors and tweezers filling the same roles.
Natural edges are uneven and can nick skin or introduce infection if not clean. No modern studies exist on shells as grooming tools.

angle.text: A shell edge scraped across the skin cuts hair near the surface, leaving a hairless, groomed look. It is a prehistoric precursor of the razor and tweezers rather than a method in common use today.

lead: Seashell hair removal is the use of sharpened shells, and flint blades, to cut or pull hair from the skin. It is described as one of the earliest forms of grooming, practiced for cleanliness and appearance before metalworking produced razors and tweezers.[1]

People using the tools aimed for the same result sought today: smooth skin and a tidy face or body. Shell edges served as scraping razors, and shell halves have been described as tweezers for pulling individual hairs, though that specific tweezer detail is less well documented than the use of flint and shells generally.[1]

No clinical studies exist. The practice is known mostly through general histories of hair removal, which also trace later methods such as pumice and razors in ancient Egypt and depilatory pastes in Greece, Rome and elsewhere.[1]

paras: General histories of hair removal say early peoples removed hair mainly for cleanliness using flint, seashells, beeswax and other tools and exfoliants, some of them harsh.[1]

Later cultures developed more refined methods: affluent ancient Egyptians used pumice and razors, and Greeks and Romans used depilatory preparations and attendants who removed hair for bathers.[1] Corrosive pastes of lime, ash and orpiment are also recorded.[1]
Natural edges are irregular, so cuts and skin irritation are plausible; no studies have measured this.
